title: MedLink: De-Identified Patient Health Record Linkage

problem.claim: Patient health records are scattered across multiple healthcare systems, making it difficult to link records belonging to the same patient across different timelines and to distinguish informative health patterns when common medical codes dominate.

gap.claim: Existing record linkage approaches primarily rely on patient identifiers, which can invade privacy and suffer from identifier discrepancies.

contributions.claim: MedLink links de-identified patient health records by matching health patterns without strictly relying on sensitive patient identifiers.
MedLink uses bi-directional health prediction to account for health progression and a prevalence-aware retrieval design to emphasize low-prevalence, informative codes during learning.
MedLink supports end-to-end training and lightweight inference for large patient databases.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report evaluating MedLink against leading baselines on the real-world MIMIC-III critical care dataset and a large health claims dataset.
The authors report that MedLink outperforms the best baseline by 4% in top-1 accuracy with 8% memory cost.
The authors report that combining MedLink with existing identifier-based linkage approaches improves their performance by up to 15%.

narrative_sequence.summary: Comprehensive patient health histories support patient care and healthcare research, but records are distributed across systems.
Identifier-based linkage has privacy and discrepancy limitations.
MedLink matches de-identified health patterns and addresses timeline differences and prevalence imbalance using bi-directional prediction and prevalence-aware retrieval.
The model is end-to-end trainable and lightweight for inference on large patient databases.
The authors report evaluation on real-world datasets, improved top-1 accuracy with low memory cost, and gains when combined with identifier-based methods.

source_observation.claim: Health records from different timelines make record matching difficult because disease progression changes the observed health patterns.

interpretation.claim: Linkage methods should model temporal progression rather than treating records as static pattern snapshots.

application.claim: For longitudinal record linkage, consider prediction objectives that use both future and past context.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether bi-directional prediction is beneficial for datasets without meaningful temporal progression.

source_observation.claim: Common medical codes can overshadow more informative low-prevalence codes, and the proposed method focuses retrieval on the latter.

interpretation.claim: Frequency-aware representation or retrieval can reduce the dominance of common but less discriminative features.

application.claim: In sparse classification or matching tasks, consider weighting or retrieving rare features more heavily when they carry greater discriminative value.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how prevalence is measured or whether low-prevalence codes are consistently informative across settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the model architecture or training objective beyond bi-directional health prediction and prevalence-aware retrieval.
The abstract does not provide dataset sizes, comparison protocols, statistical variation, or detailed error analysis.
The abstract does not report privacy guarantees or quantify the privacy risk of the linkage process.
